title: set and unordered_set
learningGoals: see that a set sorts its items

youtube.title: C++ std::set: Unique and Sorted | C++ Programming EP 74
youtube.description: In this episode you will store unique values, see that a set sorts its items and check if an insert worked, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 set and unordered_set · 0:52 A set of numbers · 1:32 From a vector to a set · 2:02 Second program · 3:02 Recap · 3:32 Bug of the Day · 4:20 Challenge · 4:40 Next episode

chapters.label: From a vector to a set

thumbnail.visual: big text "SETS" in tomato on lilac; Xecxec next to a bag where every item is different; thin black border and drop shadow.
thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a bag where every item is different

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we meet the set. It stores each value once. It is the quickest way to remove duplicates.

scenes.onScreen: "set and unordered_set": numbered lines (1. A set stores each value once; 2. A set keeps its values sorted; 3. Insert tells you if it added a new value) and an analogy card: a guest list: every name appears once, and the clerk keeps it in order
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A set stores unique values. If you insert a value twice, the second insert does nothing. A set keeps its values sorted. An unordered set is faster, but it has no order. Insert returns a pair. The second part tells you if the value was new. Think of a guest list. Every name appears once, and the clerk keeps it in order.
points: A set stores each value once
A set keeps its values sorted
Insert tells you if it added a new value

analogy.title: set and unordered_set
analogy.body: A guest list: every name appears once, and the clerk keeps it in order

scenes.onScreen: unique.cpp: a set removes duplicates and sorts
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 7] The vector has six numbers, with duplicates. [HL 8] We build a set from the whole vector. Duplicates disappear. [HL 9] The loop prints the values in sorted order. [HL 13] The output is one, three, five, nine, and the size is four.

scenes.onScreen: a flow: vector with duplicates, set builds, sorted unique values
scenes.animation: Steps drop in left to right with a pop; connecting arrows draw on; the active step glows butter
scenes.narration: The vector has six items. The set keeps each value once, and in order. That leaves four items. This is the shortest way to remove duplicates.

diagram.caption: a flow: vector with duplicates, set builds, sorted unique values

scenes.onScreen: insert.cpp: insert returns a pair with a flag
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 7] The first insert adds four. [HL 8] The second insert finds four already there. [HL 9] The second part of the result is a flag. The first flag is true, and the second is false. [HL 10] Count tells us if a value is in the set. Four is there, so one. [HL 10] Seven is not, so zero.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as insert dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints true false, and then one zero.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A set stores each value once. Two. A set keeps its values sorted. Three. Insert tells you if the value was new. Four. Count checks if a value is in the set. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A set stores each value once.
A set keeps its values sorted.
Insert tells you if the value was new.
Count checks if a value is in the set.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: Expecting duplicates
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. We count six ballots, but the program says three. A set keeps each value once. It counts the different candidates, not the votes. Use a vector, or a map of counts, when duplicates matter.

scenes.onScreen: A set told a joke twice. Nobody heard it the second time.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: A set told a joke twice. Nobody heard it the second time.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: remove the duplicates from a vector
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Read five numbers into a vector. Print them without duplicates, in sorted order. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.onScreen: Next: EP 75 · stack, queue and deque
scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: stack, queue and deque. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Program output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

Total votes: 3
bug.why: A set keeps each value once, so it counts the different values, not the total. To count every item, use a vector.

pun: "A set told a joke twice. Nobody heard it the second time."
challenge: Read five numbers into a vector. Print them without duplicates, in sorted order.
challengeAnswer: Build a set from the vector. Print every item of the set with a range-based for.
